opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the core problem is that a model is a very slippery thing to pin down. When we regulate other powerful technologies, whether it's drugs, airplanes, or nuclear reactors, there's a fairly stable object that you can test, certify, and then hold someone accountable for. With AI models, the thing you approve on Monday can be fine-tuned, quantized, merged with other models, or wrapped in agent scaffolding by Tuesday, and its capabilities can change dramatically. So what exactly did you certify?

There's also the problem that capabilities aren't really fixed properties of the weights. A lot of what a model can actually do depends on how it's prompted, what tools it's hooked up to, and how much inference-time compute you throw at it. We've seen again and again that models have latent capabilities that even their creators didn't know about until someone poked at them in the right way. So if your regulation says "this model has been evaluated and found safe," that's a pretty weak guarantee.

And once weights are released openly, the concept of a model as a regulated unit kind of evaporates, because you can't recall them. There's no equivalent of pulling a drug off pharmacy shelves.

So I think it makes more sense to think in terms of the whole system and the actors involved: who's training at what scale, what compute they're using, how the systems are deployed, and above all, what the burden of proof is. In every other industry, the company has to demonstrate to independent experts that the product is safe before it goes to market. That's the principle we need for AI too. We shouldn't treat AI companies as the one industry that gets to skip that step simply because the products are hard to define.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes models as changeable, hard to certify, and impossible to recall once weights are open, but does not identify their nature as digital bits as the obstacle.

r002.rationale: The candidate compares AI models with drugs, airplanes, and nuclear reactors; it does not liken model-level regulation to regulating computers, software, or transistors at that level of abstraction.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's helpful to step back and ask what we're actually trying to regulate. With most other technologies, the unit is pretty obvious. You regulate the drug, you regulate the airplane, you regulate the nuclear reactor. There's a physical thing, it goes through a review process, and once it's approved it does roughly what it was approved to do. AI models are weird in that respect for a few reasons.

The first is that a model isn't a product, it's more like a substrate. The same set of weights can be a tutor for kids, a coding assistant, a tool for designing bioweapons, or a persuasion engine, depending entirely on how it's prompted and what it's hooked up to. So if you regulate at the model level, you're regulating something whose behavior isn't fixed. And if you regulate at the application level, you've got thousands of applications sitting on top of a handful of models, and the dangerous capabilities live in the model, not in any particular app.

The second is that the thing itself is just a file. You can copy it, fine-tune it, strip out safety training in an afternoon with a few hundred dollars of compute. There's no equivalent of that for a nuclear reactor. So the question of what counts as "the same model" gets murky very fast. Is Llama with a safety fine-tune removed the same model Meta released? Legally, who's responsible?

The third is that capabilities emerge in ways even the developers don't predict. Companies routinely discover what their models can do after they've trained them. That makes pre-deployment evaluation a bit like trying to certify a drug when you don't know all the molecules in the pill.

So my view is that models are hard to regulate not because regulation is impossible, but because people keep reaching for the wrong analogies. I actually think the right move is to stop treating this as an exotic new problem and bring AI into the same framework as every other powerful industry: you don't get to sell it until you've shown it's safe, and the burden is on the company, not the public. Every other industry in America operates that way, from sandwich shops to pharmaceuticals. The fact that AI doesn't is a policy choice, not a law of nature.

r001.rationale: It says a model is “just a file” that can be copied and fine-tuned, making model identity and responsibility hard to regulate.

r002.rationale: It describes models as a substrate with varied uses, but does not compare model-level regulation to regulating computers, software, transistors, or similar general-purpose technologies at that level.

astra-6.text:
I think a model is a difficult unit of regulation because it’s not necessarily the model itself that determines the risk. It’s what you connect it to, what tools you give it, and how much autonomy it has. The same model might be relatively harmless if it’s just answering questions, and much more dangerous if it can execute code, move money, or control physical equipment.

There’s also a problem with drawing the boundary. You can build a system out of several models, together with ordinary software, and the capabilities of that whole system can be quite different from those of any individual component. So if your regulation only looks at the model, you can miss what actually matters.

I would focus on the system and the risks it creates. What can it do in the setting where it’s being deployed? What evidence do we have that it’s safe? And who’s responsible if something goes wrong? Models are certainly useful places to do testing, but they’re only part of the picture.

r001.rationale: The response discusses risk from a model’s tools, autonomy, and deployment setting, but does not identify digital bits as an obstacle to regulation.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare model-level regulation to regulating computers, software, transistors, or other general-purpose technologies at that level.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a model is a difficult thing to regulate because it isn’t a fixed product with a single use. The same model can be used for something wonderful or something dangerous, depending on what you connect it to, what tools you give it, and how much autonomy it has. And once the weights are out there, you can copy them, modify them, and combine them with other systems.

So I think we need to focus on capabilities and consequences. What can the actual system do? Could it help someone cause large-scale harm? And who is responsible for demonstrating that it’s safe before it’s deployed? Models are certainly part of that picture, but drawing a regulatory boundary around a model alone doesn’t capture the whole problem.

r001.rationale: The response says model weights can be copied, modified, and combined, but does not identify their being digital bits as a practical obstacle to regulation.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare regulating models at that level to regulating computers, software, transistors, or other general-purpose technologies.
